moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
moves.claimSummary: Altruistic behavior can be evolutionarily intelligible without divine programming.
moves.reasonSummary: Giving blood benefits another at a small replenishable cost, feels rewarding, and also sustains a system the donor may later need; social species can carry both cooperative and selfish traits.

inferenceSummary.conclusion: Self-sacrifice and moral concern do not require a supernatural spark, and imperfect variation is expected under evolution.

moves.speaker: William Dembski
moves.claimSummary: Evolution can be invoked for both cooperation and violence, so it does not normatively privilege altruism.
moves.reasonSummary: Accounts of rape or infanticide as adaptations illustrate that nature contains both socially attractive and brutal behaviors; design can identify intentional structure independently of whether the design appears morally optimal.

inferenceSummary.premise: Accounts of rape or infanticide as adaptations illustrate that nature contains both socially attractive and brutal behaviors; design can identify intentional structure independently of whether the design appears morally optimal.
inferenceSummary.inference: If accounts of rape or infanticide as adaptations illustrate that nature contains both socially attractive and brutal behaviors; design can identify intentional structure independently of whether the design appears morally optimal. then the stated claim materially affects the assigned burden.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: An evolutionary genealogy of bonding does not establish which evolved disposition ought to govern, while natural evil remains a challenge rather than a refutation of design.
